newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. ambassador slams Colombian anti-drug efforts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ambassador slams Colombian anti-drug efforts.

text.p: U.S. ambassador Myles Frechette caused a political storm in Colombia on Tuesday by criticising as insufficient anti-drug measures proposed by the country's legislators.
In a meeting with business leaders, Frechette criticised a watered-down bill on the extradition of drug traffickers passed last week by the senate because it would not be applied retroactively.
The proposal would shut the door on U.S. efforts to bring jailed heads of the Cali drug cartel to trial in U.S. courts.
"What has so far been approved in congress doesn't really meet international requirements nor allow Colombia to face its responsibilities on organised crime," Frechette said.

Two cabinet ministers accused Frechette of overstepping the diplomatic mark and interfering in Colombia's internal affairs. And congressmen suspended all debate on tougher penalties for traffickers in protest at what they termed interference by the U.S. envoy.

Frechette also expressed doubts about the effectiveness of two other bills currently going through congress that are meant to introduce stiffer sentences for drug crimes and confiscate the property of drug lords.

His comments were widely seen as a warning signal that Colombia would not regain certification as a U.S. ally in the drug war unless it agreed to send drug lords already in Colombian jails to stand trial in the United States.
"There are still people that ask why Frechette is called the U.S. viceroy," said Interior Minister Horacio Serpa. "It's not that he is a viceroy but he certainly feels he is one."
Justice Minister Carlos Medellin described the envoy's remarks as poorly timed and he tried to persuade congressmen to continue their debate on stiffer penalties for drug crimes.
It was unclear whether congressmen will renew debate on extradition scheduled for later this week.

The U.S. government has been unsuccessful in pressing President Ernesto Samper, who is dogged by allegations of links to drug barons, to send Colombian traffickers to stand trial in the United States. Top of the list are the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers, kingpins of the once-powerful Cali cartel.
Colombia imposed a constitutional ban on extradition in 1991 after the drug cartels waged a campaign of bombings, kidnappings and assassinations.
The proposals now before congress would not be retroactive or apply to traffickers who gave themselves up voluntarily.

Frechette's views echoed similar criticism made last week by Colombia's chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso, a fervent anti-drug crusader who said the proposals were unworkable and represented no advance in the fight against drugs.
